title: Relational Algebra Practice
description: Turn student-facing questions into precise candidate populations, quantifiers and result grains, then test none, some and every using deliberate counterexamples.
notes:
## Read the question as a result contract

Practising relational algebra means deciding which facts a question requests and composing operations that produce exactly those facts. The useful skill is not guessing a keyword from one familiar word. Read the candidate population, relationship, quantifier, filter and output roles together. A short English question can hide several decisions about missing records, repeated occurrences and the meaning of all.

Use a campus setting with students, clubs and memberships. Students identifies people. Clubs identifies possible organizations. Memberships records student-club pairs. A student can join several clubs, and a club can have many members. In the exercises, membership pairs are the accepted relationship facts; the query does not independently check an external registration system or enforce permissions to view the result.

## Identify what one row should represent

The question which students belong to a club normally requests student identities, not one row per membership occurrence. Asha in two clubs should still appear once in such a report. The question list all memberships instead requests participation facts, so two Asha rows can be correct when they represent different clubs. Choose the grain before deciding whether duplicate elimination is necessary.

Displayed names are not reliable identity. Two different students can both be named Asha, and a name-only distinct projection merges them. Keep student_id when the task asks which students. If the task really wants a set of name labels, name-only projection is appropriate. These are different result contracts, not alternative formatting choices for the same report.

## Translate some into an existence condition

Students with at least one membership in a science club require a matching relationship to some qualifying club. A join followed by distinct student projection can express the result. An EXISTS subquery can also express student membership directly without generating all qualifying participation occurrences in the outer result. Neither syntax is automatically faster for every engine and workload.

The club category filter must apply to the club associated with the tested membership. Testing whether any science club exists somewhere in the database is insufficient. Correlation connects the current student to the relevant membership and its club. An uncorrelated existence test can accidentally admit every student as soon as a single unrelated qualifying record exists.

## Translate none into absence of a qualifying witness

Students with no science-club membership means there is no membership linking that student to a science club. A student who belongs only to an arts club still qualifies. A student with no memberships also qualifies. A student who belongs to both science and arts does not qualify because the science witness is enough to violate the none condition.

This is not equivalent to finding a membership whose club category is not science. That weaker test admits the student who has both kinds because the arts membership satisfies it. The predicate must reject the existence of any forbidden qualifying relationship, rather than accepting the existence of an unrelated permitted one. Counterexamples with mixed relationships expose this mistake quickly.

## Use the full candidate universe for absence

An inner join starting from memberships cannot discover students with no membership rows at all. Begin from the students candidate population when those people belong in the answer. Then test the absence of relevant matches. This same population choice appears in questions about departments with no employees, courses with no enrollment, and products with no purchase.

A left join followed by a NULL test can express absence if the tested right-side marker is guaranteed non-NULL in actual matches. Testing an optional descriptive attribute is unsafe: a real match can have an unknown description. NOT EXISTS often makes the witness logic easier to read, but the important requirement is correct correlation and candidate preservation.

## Translate every into no missing requirement

Students who belong to every required club need a different quantifier. For each student, there must be no required club without a corresponding membership. A double NOT EXISTS formulation expresses that missing-witness test. Having at least one required membership is insufficient when several distinct clubs are required. Having no memberships is insufficient when any club is required.

If no clubs are required, every student in the stated candidate universe satisfies the universal condition. That is the empty-requirement boundary, sometimes called vacuous truth. A product that demands at least one configured requirement adds another condition. Do not silently substitute that policy while teaching the mathematical every-item interpretation. The second exercise explicitly includes students with no memberships as candidates.

## Distinguish every from exactly the required set

A student can belong to every required club and also join an extra arts club. The universal requirement still holds because no required association is missing. Exactly the required clubs is stricter: it needs both complete coverage of requirements and absence of memberships outside that set. Adding that restriction changes the requested question and must be stated explicitly.

Similarly, not every and none are different. A student missing one required club but belonging to another satisfies not every while failing none. Translate negation at the correct scope. Writing down a two-club example, with one membership present and the other absent, makes these distinctions concrete without relying on ambiguous natural-language shortcuts.

## Select operations after deciding the quantifier

Projection chooses requested roles. Selection restricts candidate facts. Joins attach related facts. Difference or an anti-existence formulation expresses absence. Division-style reasoning expresses every required relationship. Union combines compatible result sets, while intersection keeps members present in both sets. These operators answer different logical needs even when their SQL translations share familiar keywords.

Do not force a particular operator solely because the topic heading suggests it. An exercise asking for none can use a correctly scoped NOT EXISTS rather than a literal EXCEPT expression. The result contract and supported dialect decide which formulation is suitable. If an assessment requires a particular technique, result fixtures alone cannot prove that the submission used that technique.

## Preserve scope, duplicates and absence rules

The exercise identifiers are required values, so ordinary equality can compare student and club roles directly. A more complex model might make club numbers unique only within a campus. Both the relationship and its comparison would then need the campus identifier. A matching local number alone could connect different organizations and corrupt every, some and none results alike.

Repeated membership rows do not create additional distinct clubs. Existence predicates naturally ignore the number of matching occurrences, while count-based formulations need appropriate distinctness and domain filtering. Nullable comparison attributes introduce SQL unknown values, so avoid mechanically replacing NOT EXISTS with NOT IN. The precise nullability and intended meaning of missing identifiers must be included in that alternative's reasoning.

## Construct counterexamples before trusting a sample

For a none query, include a student with no memberships, one with only arts, one with only science, and one with both. The mixed case catches the tempting category-not-science error. For an every query, include complete coverage, one missing requirement, duplicate memberships, unrelated extra clubs and empty requirements. An empty students table should return no invented candidates in either task.

Also include two students sharing a name, so the output grain remains visible. Record expected results by hand from the witness rules before running the reference solution. This prevents the same mistaken SQL assumption from being copied into the expected output. Sorting by student_id makes fixture comparison deterministic without claiming that relations have an inherent display order.

## Explain why each candidate enters or leaves

A strong solution can name the witness that includes or excludes each boundary candidate. For none, a single forbidden science membership excludes the student. For every, a single missing required club excludes the student. For some, one qualifying witness is enough. Those explanations are portable reasoning tools rather than a memorized arrangement of SQL clauses.

After the result is correct, compare alternative formulations for clarity and, where relevant, measured execution behaviour. Keep logical equivalence, local reference-result checks, exact provider compatibility and access authorization separate. The practice fixtures establish recorded results over supplied synthetic inputs. They do not prove production performance, authorize source records, or close the independent review and browser verification gaps tracked for this content rebuild.

questions.question_text: What is the primary skill this topic focuses on?
options: Translating a plain-English question into the correct sequence of relational algebra operations / SQL clauses
questions.explanation: This topic is specifically about the translation skill from natural language to algebra/SQL.

questions.question_text: A question asks 'which X have NO relationship to Y' — which pattern does this typically signal?
questions.explanation: 'None of' language points to Difference (or an anti-join / NOT EXISTS), not Division.

questions.question_text: A question asks 'which X relate to ALL of Y' — which pattern does this typically signal?
questions.explanation: 'All of' language is the classic signal for the Division operation covered in 7.12.

questions.question_text: Why is confusing 'none of' with 'all of' language a common real mistake?
options: They are actually the same pattern with no meaningful difference
They point to genuinely different operations (Difference/anti-join vs. Division) that produce very different, non-interchangeable results
This confusion never actually happens in practice
Both always produce identical results regardless of which pattern is used
questions.explanation: Difference and Division answer fundamentally different questions, so mixing them up produces an incorrect query.

questions.question_text: What should be identified before choosing the operation sequence?
options: The exact column names for the final output
The candidate population, needed source relations and intended result grain
Whether to use UNION or INTERSECT
questions.explanation: Starting sources and population matter especially when absent relationships must be reported.

questions.question_text: If a question needs rows that exist in one relation but are unmatched in a related one, which operation category applies?
options: An absence pattern such as NOT EXISTS or a left join with a reliable non-NULL match-marker test
questions.explanation: An outer join alone also returns matches; an absence condition is required to isolate unmatched candidates.

questions.question_text: What is a practical benefit of breaking a complex question into 'which relations, which filter, which combination'?
options: It has no real benefit over guessing
It decomposes an intimidating question into a short, tractable sequence of the well-defined operations covered in this chapter
It guarantees the fastest possible query automatically
It removes the need to ever use a JOIN
questions.explanation: The checklist turns an overwhelming question into a manageable, step-by-step construction process.

questions.question_text: Is precisely matching the columns a question asks for (Projection) usually straightforward?
options: Yes, there is never any ambiguity
It's easy to get wrong when several plausible candidate columns exist — the exact wording of the question should be checked carefully
Projection is not actually relevant to answering questions correctly
Only Selection matters; Projection is optional
questions.explanation: Careful attention to exactly which columns were asked for avoids a common, easy-to-miss error.

questions.question_text: A student joins both science and arts. Do they have no science-club membership?
options: Yes, because they also joined arts
questions.explanation: One science witness violates none.

questions.question_text: No clubs are required. Who satisfies every required club in an explicit students universe?
options: Only students with at least two memberships
questions.explanation: There is no missing requirement for any candidate.

questions.question_text: What does at least one qualifying relationship require?
questions.explanation: Existential membership does not demand complete coverage.

questions.question_text: Which candidate can a membership-driven inner join miss?
options: A student with an ordinary matching pair
A student with a numeric key
A student with no membership rows
questions.explanation: The full population must be present before testing absence.

questions.question_text: Why is category <> science not enough to find students with no science memberships?
options: A student can have both a non-science and a science membership
The inequality is always invalid SQL
Every student has one club only
questions.explanation: Existence of a permitted occurrence does not prove absence of a forbidden one.

questions.question_text: Which marker is safe for a left-join unmatched test?
options: A right-side key guaranteed non-NULL on a real match
A constant from the left source
questions.explanation: Optional right descriptions cannot reliably distinguish padding from a match.

questions.question_text: Can an extra club disqualify a student from every-required-club membership alone?
questions.explanation: Every required is weaker than exactly the required set.

questions.question_text: A student joins one of two required clubs. Which statement is true?
options: They satisfy not every but do not satisfy none
questions.explanation: Negation scope changes the condition.

questions.question_text: Why keep student_id with repeated displayed names?
questions.explanation: Name labels can coincide for different people.

questions.question_text: What does a repeated membership establish under existence semantics?
questions.explanation: Repeated occurrences do not create another distinct obligation.

questions.question_text: What should be decided before running the reference SQL?
options: Hand-derived boundary results from the intended witness rules
An arbitrary output copied from the query
questions.explanation: Independent expected results help catch shared reasoning mistakes.

questions.question_text: When do none and every both hold for the same candidate?
options: Only if two names are equal
When the compared requirement set is empty under those quantified conditions
questions.explanation: An empty obligation domain has no existing witness and no missing required witness.

coding_problems.title: Find students with no science-club membership
coding_problems.task: Return student_id and name for every student with no membership in a club whose category is science. Include students with no memberships and students with only other categories. A student with both science and arts is excluded. Unmatched club proposals establish no science membership.
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Ben'),(3,'Chen'),(4,'Devi'); INSERT INTO clubs VALUES (10,'science'),(20,'arts'); INSERT INTO memberships VALUES (1,10),(1,20),(2,20),(3,10);
constraints: students defines the full candidate universe.
Only memberships joined to a science club are forbidden witnesses.
hints: Correlate an absence test to the current student.
The club category belongs inside the forbidden-witness search.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT s.student_id,s.name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM memberships m JOIN clubs c ON c.club_id=m.club_id WHERE m.student_id=s.student_id AND c.category='science') ORDER BY s.student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: Only a science membership witness excludes a candidate; a separate arts witness cannot cancel it.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Asha'); INSERT INTO clubs VALUES (10,'science'),(20,'arts'); INSERT INTO memberships VALUES (1,10),(1,20),(2,20),(2,20);
INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Asha'); INSERT INTO memberships VALUES (1,99);

coding_problems.title: Find every candidate covering all required clubs
coding_problems.task: Return student_id once for every supplied student with membership in every distinct required_clubs club_id. Extra memberships are allowed. Empty requirements qualify every supplied student, even with no memberships.
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO students VALUES (1),(2),(3); INSERT INTO required_clubs VALUES (10),(20); INSERT INTO memberships VALUES (1,10),(1,20),(1,99),(2,10);
constraints: Student identifiers define an explicit candidate universe.
edge_cases: Duplicate requirements are the same obligation.
Duplicate memberships cannot replace a missing required club.
hints: Look for a required club missing for the current student.
Keep a student only when no missing witness exists.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT s.student_id FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM required_clubs r WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM memberships m WHERE m.student_id=s.student_id AND m.club_id=r.club_id)) ORDER BY s.student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The double absence condition is universal coverage over the supplied students universe.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO students VALUES (1),(2); INSERT INTO required_clubs VALUES (10),(10),(20); INSERT INTO memberships VALUES (1,10),(1,20),(2,10),(2,10),(2,99);
